confidence_note: Checked against the archive.org full text. The old Federer/LeBron/Sharapova material is not in the book and was removed. The Iguodala figures are one player's tracker data presented by Walker, not a controlled study. Walker's book has been criticised for overstating some numbers, so figures are kept with their scope. The injury chart's exact percentages are not reproduced.
facts: Walker's lab found that overnight motor-skill gains were tied to stage 2 NREM sleep spindles, especially in the last two hours of an eight-hour night, for example 5 to 7 a.m. after falling asleep at 11 p.m.
Those last two hours are the ones many people cut to get a jump on the day; Walker pictures the coach who trains athletes late and wakes them early.
Usain Bolt on many occasions napped in the hours before breaking the world record and before Olympic finals he won.
Walker tells national teams sleep is a powerful, legal performance enhancer; with under eight hours, and especially under six, time to physical exhaustion drops 10 to 30 percent.
A 2014 study of competitive young athletes found chronic short sleep across a season predicted a much higher injury risk.

Walker shows teams tracker data from NBA player Andre Iguodala: on nights of more than eight hours versus less, 12% more minutes played and 29% more points per minute; with less sleep, 37% more turnovers and 45% more fouls.
Walker tells teams that sleep after a game matters as much: it speeds recovery from inflammation, stimulates muscle repair and restocks glucose and glycogen.
In 2015 the International Olympic Committee published a consensus statement on the essential need for sleep in athletic development.
Walker notes that very small differences often separate a gold medal from last place.

Other groups found the same local sleep-and-learning effect; studies have since shown sleep improving motor skills of junior, amateur and elite athletes in sports including tennis, basketball, football, soccer and rowing.
scene_details: the 5 to 7 a.m. window after an 11 p.m. bedtime
the coach waking athletes early for practice
tension: The hour an athlete sacrifices for an early session is the hour in which the brain finishes the practice.
opening_idea: Open with Usain Bolt sleeping in the hours before an Olympic final.

lessons.idea: Protect the end of the night after a day of learning a skill, because that is where the practice is finished.
lessons.anchor: Spindles in the last two hours; the early-practice coach.
lessons.example: A new nurse learning to place IV lines sets her alarm later the night after training instead of rising early to review.

reflect_final: After the next day you spend learning something physical or new, what would you have to move to sleep the last full hour of the night?

use_cases.situation: A coach or manager schedules early sessions after late ones.
use_cases.move: Mention that Walker found the last two hours of sleep carry the motor-skill gains, and suggest a later start once.

use_cases.situation: Your teenager has a game and wants to stay up.
use_cases.move: Tell them Bolt napped before finals and suggest one earlier night before the match.

use_cases.situation: Learning an instrument or a sport yourself.
use_cases.move: On a practice day, skip the early alarm and notice the next session.

pocket_idea: The last two hours of sleep finish what practice started; an early alarm cuts them.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Usain Bolt took naps in the hours before breaking world records.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Walker found skill gains come from sleep spindles in the last two hours of the night, the hours people cut. Iguodala's tracker: more than eight hours meant 29% more points per minute and fewer fouls.
conversation_variants.question_idea: What do you cut first when the day is busy?
